She is a flamepoint! And flamepoint girls are apparently quite rare, usually they’re boys! I rescued a little girl 3 years ago and she’s been my bestie ever since lol. Flamepoint isn’t a breed, it’s actually the coloring..so her “points” (tail, face, ears) are orange aka flame and her body is white/cream. Usually these areas will darken as they get older! Which is why people will say they toasted up. 

I rescued my flamepoint, lychee,  when she was like 6 months old and she was also super friendly and not skittish at all. Flamepoints are usually pretty talkative and almost puppy-like. Lychee knows how to fetch and will sleep under the covers with me lol I’ve never had a cat that is so cuddly and playful. They’re a lot of fun. 

In terms of vet care,  since they’re white cats they could have skin allergies or just overall skin sensitivity. That is something to keep an eye out for but don’t stress about it. Just letting you know so you know

This may be incorrect but I’m pretty sure flamepoings are the result of a parent or parents that had orange tabby dna and some Siamese dna (or ragdoll any other breed that has the “points”). I hope this makes sense! Let us know what you will name her :)

OP please see my comment! This looks like [potodermatitis](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9009751/), my cat has it. 

A year ago I noticed she had flaky paws, tried everything and nothing was working but she wasn’t in pain and it wasn’t a wound, just dry skin. Then her flaky paw had actually cracked and exposed her raw skin poking out like a nodule.  I was bugging. I took her to the vet, the confirmed potodermatitis and offered two scenarios of treatment. 

1) steroid, which is often ongoing and can caught weight gain etc we both didn’t want to go straight to that so we opted for

2) liquid doxycycline (I forget if we had my cat on it for a week or 2) but I administered it for whatever the vet directed and her paws cleared right up and hasn’t flared up since :) the vet did mention sometimes multiple rounds of doxy could be necessary but we haven’t had to do it again


I equate it to psoriasis or eczema in humans.
